item.title: Taiwan economy to benefit from reunification
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
Taiwan economy to benefit from reunification MA XUEJING/CHINA DAILY Editor's note:The Taiwan question is a key focus for China and the international community. China Daily is publishing a series of reports to track hot Taiwan-related topics and address disinformation from the Democratic Progressive Party administration. Taiwan's reunification with the Chinese mainland could reshape the island's economic landscape by providing greater policy certainty, strengthening energy security and accelerating infrastructure upgrades, analysts said. On Oct 25 last year, marked as Taiwan Recovery Day, Wang Huning, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, outlined seven areas in which Taiwan could see improvements following peaceful reunification. The seven areas include stronger economic development, enhanced energy and resource security, improved infrastructure, greater security, expanded external exchanges, improved livelihoods, and richer cultural and spiritual lives for Taiwan residents. Analysts said the mainland's economic scale and ongoing cross-Strait exchanges have demonstrated the potential for deeper integration in these areas. Industrial complementarity The mainland and Taiwan share complementary advantages across their industrial and supply chains, said Tang Hua, an associate professor at Xiamen University in Fujian province. "For Taiwan enterprises, from creative ideas to finished products, and from research and development to sales, efficient supporting resources are available on the mainland," Tang said. Despite the Democratic Progressive Party's efforts to restrict cross-Strait exchanges and cooperation, demand for such cooperation remains strong in Taiwan, while industrial ties across the Strait continue to deepen, according to trade data and industry assessments. According to the General Administration of Customs, cross-Strait trade totaled about $185 billion from January to June this year, up 25.3 percent year-on-year. The mainland's exports to Taiwan reached $51.88 billion, an increase of 32.9 percent, while its imports from Taiwan stood at $133.15 billion, up 22.5 percent year-on-year. To date, 67 Taiwan enterprises have been listed on mainland stock exchanges. The mainland's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) further encourages cross-Strait economic cooperation. According to the plan, the mainland will continue to introduce policies benefiting Taiwan compatriots and enterprises, support Taiwan businesses in developing on the mainland and encourage their participation in national regional development strategies and the Belt and Road Initiative. The plan also calls for building a common market across the Taiwan Strait and encouraging Taiwan-funded enterprises to list on mainland exchanges. In August, Taiwan's federation of industries, the island's largest industrial and business association, released its annual white paper, calling on the DPP authorities to study the industrial trends outlined in the 15th Five-Year Plan. The move, it said, would help Taiwan businesses better understand changes in the mainland market and identify future business opportunities. The white paper described the mainland market as "an indispensable and key source of revenue for many Taiwan enterprises". As the mainland builds global competitiveness in emerging technology sectors, it generates substantial demand in new areas and creates opportunities for Taiwan businesses with technological advantages to explore new markets, the federation said. The mainland has one of the world's most complete industrial systems, while Taiwan has technological advantages in fields such as semiconductors and precision manufacturing, Tang said. "The two sides can therefore form a complementary structure featuring Taiwan-based research and development combined with mainland manufacturing, or Taiwan's technologies paired with the mainland's market," she added. Zhong Houtao, a professor at the University of International Relations in Beijing, said Taiwan's economy would be more resilient to external shocks with the support of the mainland market. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world's largest contract chipmaker, has increased investment and relocated manufacturing capacity to the United States amid US tariff pressures, according to reports. The move has raised concerns in Taiwan that the relocation could weaken a key pillar of the island's industrial sector. Zhong said Taiwan's economic structure remained vulnerable because of its reliance on external resources and markets. "It will encounter challenges if problems arise either in the supply of raw materials or in market demand," he said. "With the mainland as a strong support, Taiwan would be better positioned to safeguard its own interests and gain greater confidence, and no longer need to be constrained by external forces," Zhong added. Energy security Peaceful reunification could help diversify and optimize Taiwan's energy mix, contributing to a more stable energy supply for residents and industries, experts said. Taiwan currently relies heavily on energy imports because of its limited natural resources, with shipments mainly transported through a concentrated network of maritime routes. In 2025, imports accounted for 95.4 percent of the island's oil consumption. Its energy mix consists mainly of crude oil, liquefied natural gas and coal, while its current natural gas reserves are sufficient to cover about 11 days of consumption. Rising geopolitical tensions in the Middle East have heightened concerns in Taiwan over energy supply security and raw material costs. The island has also experienced several power outages and rising prices for plastic materials this year, affecting daily life and industrial operations. Zhong said Taiwan's economic foundations could face significant challenges if external energy supplies were disrupted by global or regional instability. The concentration of energy transportation routes makes the island's energy security more vulnerable, Tang said, noting that disruptions to critical maritime routes could put its energy supply under considerable pressure. She added that Taiwan's energy security was also affected by policy decisions. The DPP authorities' decision to phase out nuclear power before renewable energy sources were fully developed, she said, reflected a greater emphasis on political considerations than on technical assessments. Relying on policy preferences rather than a balanced assessment of energy needs could create systemic risks for the island's energy security, Zhong said. In contrast, the mainland has developed the world's largest and fastest-growing renewable energy system, with total installed renewable energy capacity reaching 2.34 billion kilowatts by the end of 2025, according to the National Energy Administration. The mainland's total electricity consumption surpassed 10 trillion kilowatt-hours for the first time in 2025, without power rationing or price increases, according to official data. "The mainland's diversified energy mix and rapid development of renewable energy sources, including wind and solar power, could help provide a more stable power supply for Taiwan, while reducing the island's reliance on energy imports and maritime transportation," Tang said. Greater cross-Strait energy connectivity could also help lower electricity costs and provide a more stable power supply for energy-intensive industries in Taiwan, boosting investment and employment, she added. Upgraded infrastructure The mainland's infrastructure development has drawn considerable attention in Taiwan in recent years, with many visitors from the island impressed by proposed projects such as the Xiamen-Jinmen Bridge, a cross-sea link connecting Jinmen county in Taiwan and Xiamen in Fujian. Once completed, the bridge will shorten travel time between Jinmen and Xiamen to less than 20 minutes. It will also provide more convenient access to the newly built Xiang'an International Airport in Xiamen, facilitating travel for Jinmen residents. The project, however, has not been approved by the DPP authorities. At a regular news conference in March, Zhu Fenglian, a spokeswoman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said that "peaceful reunification will become the starting point for new and upgraded infrastructure in Taiwan". She added that Taiwan residents would be able to drive to Beijing via highways connecting the two sides after reunification. Zhong said Taiwan could draw on the mainland's extensive experience in infrastructure construction. Citing the mainland's high-speed railway network, he said its experience could provide a reference for Taiwan, including in the construction of a high-speed rail loop around the island. The mainland's transportation infrastructure expertise could also help address challenges in Taiwan's east-west transport links arising from its mountainous terrain, he added. The mainland has advantages in undertaking large-scale infrastructure projects and coordinating resources on a massive scale, while its infrastructure planning places people's needs at the center, Tang said. Beyond transportation, infrastructure in fields such as energy, agriculture, forestry, water conservancy and urban renewal could also be rebuilt and upgraded after reunification, Zhu said. The mainland has already provided practical support in water supply. Since 2018, Fujian has supplied water to Jinmen county. As of July 1, Fujian had delivered more than 50 million metric tons of water to the county, accounting for 87 percent of its daily water supply. Wang Hailiang, director of the Shanghai Institute for East Asian Studies, said existing obstacles between the two sides had made it difficult to fully address and protect the interests and needs of ordinary people. "Under reunification, the country could provide Taiwan with more comprehensive support and safeguards through coordinated institutions and mechanisms," he said. Shi Xuefancontributed to this story.

item.title: Xu Clan Members from Taiwan Return to Jiaoling to Trace Roots and Honor Ancestors
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
Xu Clan Members from Taiwan Return to Jiaoling to Trace Roots and Honor Ancestors Source: Taiwan.cnUpdated: 2026-10-16
Oct 16(Taiwan.cn)—From October 9 to 10, a 32-member delegation from the Xu Clan Association of New Taipei City, Taiwan, and the Guo Xinggong Xu Clan Association returned to their ancestral home in Jiaoling for root-tracing, ancestor worship, and exchange activities. Long-separated clan relatives from both sides of the Taiwan Strait reunited, sharing the profound bond of common ancestry. On October 10, a grand ancestor worship ceremony was held. Early that morning, the clan group from Taiwan traveled to Yanjishan for the memorial rite. At the roadside, a stone carving bears the three powerful characters “Yan Gui Lai,” meaning “Swallows Return Home.” The imagery of “Beneath Yanjishan, swallows return to their nests; wanderers come back to their homeland” touched everyone present. Dressed in proper ceremonial attire, the group ascended the mountain path step by step to the ancestral tomb and completed the worship ritual following traditional etiquette. After the ceremony, the clansmen descended the mountain and visited the Xu Ancestral Hall and Dalu Bei Ancestral Shrine in succession. They paid homage to their forebears in accordance with rites, remembering the merits of their ancestors who pioneered and established their settlement. This homecoming ancestor worship event of the Xu clan constitutes a cross-Strait journey to trace ancestral roots, as well as an emotional gathering bound by shared blood. The Taiwan Strait cannot sever kinship ties, nor can time dilute this rooted affection. Taking clan kinship as the link and hometown sentiment as the bridge, the event further deepened and enhanced the fellowship between compatriots across the Strait. It once again bears witness to the shared cultural heritage and blood connection between the two sides of the Taiwan Strait.(Jointly reported by Taiwan.cn and the Taiwan Affairs Office of Meizhou) Related Stories

item.title: Taiwan Compatriot Returns to Hometown to Seek Relatives and Honor Ancestors, Experiencing the Bond of Blood
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
Taiwan Compatriot Returns to Hometown to Seek Relatives and Honor Ancestors, Experiencing the Bond of Blood Source: Taiwan.cnUpdated: 2026-10-16
Oct 16(Taiwan.cn)—From September 24 to 29, Ms. Zhang Huilan, a compatriot from Taiwan, led a six-person group back to Xiangcheng County, Xuchang City, to seek relatives and pay homage to ancestors, fulfilling her long-cherished dream of a cross-Strait family reunion. Ms. Zhang Huilan is the daughter of Zhang Sheng'en, a veteran who moved to Taiwan. After her father passed away, she long harbored the wish to return to her hometown to look for her relatives. Through the joint efforts of all parties, Ms. Zhang's homecoming trip to trace her roots finally materialized. Welcomed by relatives and friends, Ms. Zhang and her entourage conducted root-tracing and ancestor worship activities at Sanligou Community, Cigou Subdistrict, Xiangcheng County, and at the ancestral tomb. They also visited scenic spots such as Ziyun Mountain and Shoushan Park. While enjoying the beautiful scenery, the closely related family members were immersed in the deep bonds of kinship. They talked about past stories and shared their visions for the future. Through this root-tracing trip, Ms. Zhang gained a deeper understanding of her family history, witnessed the new progress in her hometown's economic and social development, and felt a spiritual bond and sense of belonging to her ancestral home. An official from the Xuchang Taiwan Affairs Office stated that the office will use this root-seeking and ancestor worship activity as an opportunity to continue building bridges for exchanges between compatriots across the Taiwan Strait and serving as an emotional bond. It will help sustain the everlasting kinship between the two sides and contribute to the peaceful development of cross-Strait relations and the complete reunification of the motherland.(Jointly reported by Taiwan.cn and the Taiwan Affairs Office of Xuchang) Related Stories

item.title: Mainland to sanction company linked to "Taiwan independence" secessionist: spokesperson
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
Mainland to sanction company linked to "Taiwan independence" secessionist: spokesperson BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese mainland will impose sanctions on a company used by the father of die-hard "Taiwan independence" secessionist Shen Pao-yang to continue business dealings with mainland enterprises and evade earlier penalties, a mainland spokesperson said on Wednesday. Chen Binhua, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular press conference that the mainland had announced sanctions in June 2025 against Sicuens International Co., Ltd., headed by Shen Tu-cheng, Shen Pao-yang's father. An investigation found that Shen Tu-cheng had continued trade and business cooperation with mainland companies under the name of another company, VWAY, to evade the sanctions and obtain economic benefits, Chen said. The mainland will not allow companies associated with die-hard "Taiwan independence" secessionists to profit from the mainland, Chen said, adding that VWAY would be barred from any dealings with mainland organizations, enterprises and individuals. Asked to comment on the appearance of Kevin Tsai, a well-known Taiwanese entertainer active on the mainland, at the inauguration ceremony for the campaign headquarters of Shen Pao-yang, a Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) candidate for Taipei mayor, Chen said the mainland respects and protects the legitimate rights of Taiwan compatriots to freedom of speech and expression, but stressed that there can be no ambiguity on fundamental issues. Chen said Taiwan is an inalienable part of China and the one-China principle is a broad international consensus and a shared political foundation for people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait. Noting that Shen Pao-yang's actions were notorious, Chen said the mainland firmly opposes all forms of "Taiwan independence" separatist activities. "No one or force can, while reaping the benefits from the mainland's development, collude with 'Taiwan independence' separatist forces," Chen noted. In response to another question about Taiwanese entertainers posting greetings to the motherland during the National Day holiday, Chen said such patriotic expressions were natural for Taiwan compatriots, adding that the mainland fully recognized and supported them. Chen criticized the DPP authorities for repeatedly threatening and intimidating Taiwanese entertainers, saying such actions only deeply hurt the patriotic sentiments of people in Taiwan.

item.title: Chinese mainland blasts Taiwan authorities' separatist rhetoric regarding history
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
Chinese mainland blasts Taiwan authorities' separatist rhetoric regarding history BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday criticized the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities in Taiwan, saying they had unscrupulously distorted history and hyped separatist rhetoric based on a warped version of history. Such rhetoric on history revealed the DPP authorities' true intention of inciting cross-Strait confrontation, said Chen Binhua, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, when responding to a media question on Taiwan authorities' and Lai Ching-te's remarks regarding the history of World War II. It also showed the DPP authorities' ignorance of history and betrayal of the ancestors, Chen said. The Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression was the first to break out and lasted the longest in the World Anti-Fascist War, or World War II, resulting in over 35 million Chinese military and civilian casualties from 1931 to 1945. The victory of the war and the recovery of Taiwan from Japanese occupation are great victories achieved by the Chinese people, including those in Taiwan, at the cost of blood and lives, Chen noted. Taiwan's liberation from the shackles of Japan's colonial rule and its return to the motherland represent an important outcome of the Chinese people's victory in fighting Japanese aggressors, and form an integral part of the post-World War II international order, Chen said. It's a historical memory the Chinese people across the Taiwan Strait should never forget, said Chen, urging compatriots in Taiwan to see the true face of the DPP authorities and stand on the right side of history. Following the Chinese people's victory in the war of resistance against Japanese aggressors, a full-blown civil war broke out between the forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT). In 1949, the remnants of the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China was founded under the leadership of the CPC. This unresolved civil war and foreign interference have left the two sides of the Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation, but the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed. The real status quo across the Taiwan Strait is that there is only one China in the world and that Taiwan is a part of China, Chen said. By promoting a false narrative of "democracy versus authoritarianism," stoking cross-Strait confrontation, or attempting to pursue "Taiwan independence" through military means and by relying on foreign forces, the DPP authorities will only gradually drag Taiwan into a dangerous situation and bring great disaster to the people in Taiwan, Chen noted.

item.title: Mainland says separatism undermines cross-Strait peace and stability
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
Mainland says separatism undermines cross-Strait peace and stability A Chinese mainland spokesman on Wednesday rejected remarks by former Taiwan leader Tsai Ing-wen on cross-Strait relations, saying that the pursuit of "Taiwan independence" is the root cause of tensions across the Taiwan Strait. Responding to Tsai's recent remarks during a visit to the United States, Chen Binhua, spokesman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said the status quo across the Taiwan Strait is that "there is only one China in the world and Taiwan is part of China". Tsai said Taiwan residents have reached a consensus on maintaining the cross-Strait status quo and avoiding unnecessary provocations, adding that Taiwan would safeguard its "democracy and security". Chen accused the Democratic Progressive Party authorities of clinging to a separatist position in pursuit of "Taiwan independence" while using the banner of "democracy" and "peace" to collude with external forces, pursue separatism and provoke confrontation, thereby undermining peace and stability across the Strait. "'Taiwan independence' is incompatible with peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait," Chen said, adding that only by abandoning separatist positions and recognizing the one-China principle and the 1992 Consensus could peace across the Strait and stability in Taiwan be ensured. A recent Reuters report cited US officials as saying that the possibility of the Chinese mainland taking military action against Taiwan before 2028 had decreased. In response, the DPP authorities said the mainland's alleged intention to "use force" against Taiwan had never changed and would not be abandoned regardless of which party governed the island. Commenting on the remarks, Chen said the DPP authorities' adherence to a separatist position in pursuit of "Taiwan independence" remained the root cause of tensions and instability across the Strait. "China must achieve reunification, and it is an inevitable outcome. This is a historical trend that no individual or force can stop," Chen said.

item.title: Mainland denies Taiwan's claims of 'transnational suppression' in US surveillance case
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14
Mainland denies Taiwan's claims of 'transnational suppression' in US surveillance case The Chinese mainland on Wednesday rejected accusations from Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party authorities of "transnational suppression" regarding the alleged surveillance of Lai Ching-te's son in the United States, describing them as groundless claims fabricated to provoke cross-Strait tensions for political gain. According to media reports, the US Federal Bureau of Investigation recently arrested a US woman who allegedly surveilled Lai's son in the US at the direction of the Chinese mainland. Chen Binhua, spokesman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said on Wednesday that he had no information about the matter. The DPP authorities described the case as "transnational suppression" and stated they were considering revisions to the so-called "anti-infiltration act" in response. Chen said the mainland firmly opposes the DPP authorities' collusion with external forces to make groundless accusations and spread falsehoods. He criticized the authorities for using "anti-China" rhetoric to fuel confrontation and provoke cross-Strait tensions for political gain. "Such sinister schemes and despicable practices cannot deceive Taiwan residents and will only be met with opposition and condemnation," Chen said.

item.title: Chinese mainland spokesperson slams Lai Ching-te's flattering remarks on Japan
item.description:
Published: 2026-02-11
Chinese mainland spokesperson slams Lai Ching-te's flattering remarks on Japan Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-02-11
BEIJING, Feb. 11 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday denounced Taiwan authorities led by Lai Ching-te for ignoring the heinous crimes committed by Japan during its colonial rule over Taiwan, describing their flattering remarks toward Japan as utterly disgraceful. Zhu Fenglian, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks in response to a media inquiry about Lai's intention to work with Japan to "deal with regional challenges." Zhu also urged the Japanese side to retract Sanae Takaichi's erroneous remarks on Taiwan, handle Taiwan-related issues prudently, and abide by the one-China principle with concrete actions. item.title: Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges
item.description:
Published: 2026-02-11
Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges BEIJING, Feb. 11 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson has condemned Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities for imposing restrictions and obstacles on cross-Strait exchanges in pursuit of their "Taiwan independence" agenda and selfish gains. The DPP authorities, led by Lai Ching-te, are the biggest obstacle to cross-Strait interactions and their acts have drawn strong criticism from various sectors in Taiwan, Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular press briefing on Wednesday. Zhu expressed the hope that Taiwan compatriots will firmly oppose the retrogressive actions of the DPP authorities and promote exchanges and cooperation across the Taiwan Strait in various fields. She noted that cross-Strait flight routes have been disrupted due to interference from the DPP authorities, with previously operated destinations yet to resume normal operations. In 2025, the average passenger load factor on cross-Strait routes reached 80 percent, reflecting the strong need for direct flights between the two sides of the Strait, Zhu said. "We hope that the Taiwan side will heed public opinion and lift unreasonable restrictions on cross-Strait air transport as soon as possible," she added.

item.title: Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for hyping up security risks of mainland apps
item.description:
Published: 2026-01-29
Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for hyping up security risks of mainland apps Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-01-29
BEIJING, Jan. 28 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday criticized Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities for hyping up the so-called information security risks of applications from the mainland. Zhang Han, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, stated at a press conference that the DPP moves have deprived people in Taiwan, especially the youth, of their right to know and the freedom to use social networking platforms. Noting that such moves reveal the fear and insecurity of the DPP authorities, Zhang said they will have to face the dire consequences of their wayward actions.
